members.summary: Richard Frayne’s research advances quantitative magnetic resonance imaging methods and translates them into tools for vascular and neurological imaging. Early contributions include phase-contrast flow measurement and the co-development of 3D TRICKS for time-resolved contrast-enhanced MR angiography. Later collaborative work expanded into cerebrovascular and stroke imaging, automated perfusion and permeability imaging for high-grade glioma, quantitative imaging in epilepsy and persistent post-concussion symptoms, and longitudinal normative MRI resources. Across recent publications, Frayne’s role is frequently senior or collaborative, supporting multidisciplinary teams that connect MRI physics, image analysis and clinically interpretable biomarkers.

contributions.title: Quantitative flow and angiography
contributions.highlight: Foundational quantitative MRI and time-resolved angiography methods.
contributions.text: Contributed foundational methods for phase-contrast velocity measurement and co-authored 3D TRICKS, which enabled time-resolved 3D contrast-enhanced MR angiography.

contributions.title: Cerebrovascular and stroke imaging
contributions.highlight: Quantitative assessment of blood flow, diffusion and perfusion.
contributions.text: Advanced acquisition and analysis methods for cerebral blood flow, diffusion and perfusion imaging, strengthening quantitative assessment in acute stroke and cerebrovascular disease.

contributions.title: Translational brain imaging
contributions.highlight: Applications spanning glioma, epilepsy and concussion.
contributions.text: Extended quantitative MRI into glioma permeability imaging, temporal-lobe epilepsy relaxometry and exploratory concussion susceptibility mapping through multidisciplinary collaborations.

contributions.title: Normative data and generalization
contributions.highlight: Longitudinal reference data and multi-site MRI methods.
contributions.text: Helped build longitudinal quantitative-MRI reference data and more generalizable multi-site image-analysis and reconstruction approaches for aging and neurological research.

research_through_line.headline: From MRI methods to clinically useful measurement
research_through_line.text: Richard Frayne’s work has consistently translated technical advances in MRI into quantitative tools for studying blood flow, brain disease, aging and neurodegeneration.

current_direction.headline: Reliable AI across real-world variation
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward AI-supported reconstruction and analysis that can recognize uncertainty and remain dependable across different scanners, datasets and pathological findings.

details.text: In brain MR reconstruction, all-coil designs improved in-distribution performance, while coil-combined designs generalized better to unseen pathological scans. Models trained only on healthy data performed worse on pathology and tended to in-paint lesions with healthy-looking anatomy, while uncertainty estimates rose in pathological regions.

That AI work connects back to Frayne’s longer-running interest in quantitative biomarkers across aging and disease. The Calgary Normative Study was designed to characterize age effects, precision and repeatability of quantitative MR biomarkers over the adult lifespan while serving as a shared comparison resource for disease cohorts. Newer resting-state and white matter papers extend that platform into graph-based brain aging analyses and automated WMH severity scoring with uncertainty-aware models.
emphasis: quantitative biomarkers across aging and disease

current_direction.conclusion: Overall, Richard Frayne’s research footprint at the University of Calgary is best summarized as MRI method development translated into vascular brain disease, aging and neurodegeneration research, with a recent expansion into robust, uncertainty-aware AI for MR analysis and reconstruction.
conclusion_emphasis: MRI method development translated into vascular brain disease, aging and neurodegeneration research
robust, uncertainty-aware AI for MR analysis and reconstruction

members.summary: Michael Hill’s research combines clinical epidemiology, acute stroke trials, neuroimaging and health-system implementation to improve reperfusion treatment and outcomes after ischemic stroke.

contributions.title: Reperfusion trials and thrombectomy
contributions.text: Contributed to multicentre trials evaluating endovascular thrombectomy, including its longer-term benefits for patients with large established infarcts.

contributions.title: Imaging-guided prognosis
contributions.text: Helped connect baseline imaging features—including brain frailty and stroke-related CT markers—with functional outcome and expected benefit from thrombectomy.

contributions.title: Stroke systems and equitable access
contributions.text: Extended stroke research into treatment delivery, examining workflow improvement and geographic or socioeconomic barriers to timely reperfusion care.

contributions.title: Acute-trial consent methods
contributions.text: Examined consent approaches suited to time-critical stroke trials, including the acceptability of advance consent among Canadian research ethics leaders.

research_through_line.headline: From acute stroke evidence to effective care
research_through_line.text: Michael Hill’s work combines clinical trials, epidemiology and imaging to determine who benefits from reperfusion treatment and how that treatment can be delivered more effectively.

current_direction.headline: Broader treatment with more individualized selection
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward expanding thrombectomy to more complex stroke populations while refining imaging-based prognosis, long-term outcome assessment and equitable access to treatment.
current_direction.basis: Synthesized from the cited recent publications; not presented as a researcher-declared plan.

members.summary: Carolyn Emery’s research uses sport-injury epidemiology, longitudinal cohorts and prevention research to reduce concussion and musculoskeletal injury among youth athletes and translate evidence into practice and policy.

contributions.title: Pediatric concussion evidence
contributions.text: Contributed to pediatric sport-concussion guidance and large prospective studies connecting clinical concussion assessment with emerging blood-based biomarkers.

contributions.title: Sex-responsive injury prevention
contributions.text: Quantified sex-related differences in youth-sport injury and concussion and helped evaluate prevention strategies for female, woman and girl athletes.

contributions.title: Policy and implementation
contributions.text: Advanced prevention beyond efficacy studies by examining how sport rules, implementation processes and front-line reporting shape real-world injury reduction.

contributions.title: Long-term consequences of youth injury
contributions.text: Extended injury surveillance into longer-term outcomes, including the lived effects of adolescent concussion and persistent symptoms following serious youth-sport ankle injury.

research_through_line.headline: From injury surveillance to prevention in practice
research_through_line.text: Carolyn Emery’s work translates population-level injury evidence into prevention strategies, clinical guidance and sport-policy changes intended to keep young athletes active and safe.

current_direction.headline: More inclusive and implementation-ready prevention
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward sex- and gender-responsive prevention, objective concussion biomarkers, implementation science and longer-term evaluation of outcomes after youth-sport injury.

members.summary: Gerald Zamponi’s research links ion-channel biophysics and regulation to pain mechanisms, neurological disease and the development of non-opioid therapeutic strategies.

contributions.title: Calcium channels as therapeutic targets
contributions.text: Established voltage-gated calcium channels as mechanistic and pharmacological targets across pain and other neurological or psychiatric disorders.

contributions.title: Channel regulation and pain sensitivity
contributions.text: Connected molecular regulation of calcium channels with pain behaviour, including human and experimental evidence linking USP5–CaV3.2 signaling to pain sensitivity.

contributions.title: Disease-associated channel variants
contributions.text: Used electrophysiology and structural modeling to clarify how pathogenic calcium-channel variants alter function in severe neurodevelopmental disease.

contributions.title: Circuit mechanisms of chronic pain
contributions.text: Extended molecular pain research into brain-circuit function by examining how injury changes descending pain-modulatory pathways.

research_through_line.headline: From ion-channel mechanisms to pain therapeutics
research_through_line.text: Gerald Zamponi’s work connects molecular and cellular studies of ion channels to circuit-level explanations of pain and opportunities for therapeutic intervention.

current_direction.headline: Precision mechanisms for non-opioid pain control
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward integrating channel genetics, regulatory proteins, circuit physiology and next-generation channel modulators to identify more selective approaches to pain treatment.

members.summary: Nils Daniel Forkert’s research develops medical-image analysis and machine-learning methods that extract biomarkers, predict outcomes and support precision decision-making across neurological and other clinical applications.

contributions.title: Cerebrovascular image analysis
contributions.text: Developed computational methods for combining vascular anatomy and blood-flow imaging and for modeling treatment response in acute ischemic stroke.

contributions.title: Multimodal outcome prediction
contributions.text: Combined clinical metadata with complex imaging to predict both tissue injury and functional outcomes, particularly in acute stroke and treatment planning.

contributions.title: Trustworthy medical imaging AI
contributions.text: Investigated privacy vulnerability and demographic or technical bias in deep-learning models, providing frameworks for safer evaluation of medical imaging AI.

contributions.title: Scalable precision phenotyping
contributions.text: Applied machine learning to high-dimensional phenotypes and advanced distributed or self-supervised learning approaches that reduce dependence on centralized, extensively labeled datasets.

research_through_line.headline: From complex images to clinically useful predictions
research_through_line.text: Nils Daniel Forkert’s work uses computational imaging methods to turn multimodal medical data into quantitative biomarkers and patient-specific predictions intended to support research and clinical decisions.

current_direction.headline: More trustworthy and transferable medical AI
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward multimodal and distributed models that address bias, privacy, limited annotation and generalizability while expanding prediction across diseases, organs and time.

members.summary: Paul Kubes’s research uses intravital imaging to reveal how immune cells move, communicate and adapt within living tissues during infection, inflammation, thrombosis and repair.

contributions.title: Intravital imaging of immunity
contributions.text: Advanced intravital microscopy as a way to observe rapid, organ-specific immune-cell and microvascular behaviour that cannot be captured by static tissue measurements alone.

contributions.title: Leukocyte trafficking mechanisms
contributions.text: Clarified how adhesion molecules, chemokines and other guidance signals coordinate leukocyte recruitment within distinct vascular and tissue environments.

contributions.title: Liver-resident immune adaptation
contributions.text: Revealed how liver macrophage organization and identity change during fibrosis, including compensatory multicellular structures that restore bacterial clearance.

contributions.title: Immunothrombosis and tissue repair
contributions.text: Connected neutrophil extracellular traps and recruited monocytes with two sides of host defence: thrombotic injury and the coordinated repair of infected tissue.

research_through_line.headline: Seeing immune behaviour inside living tissues
research_through_line.text: Paul Kubes’s work uses direct visualization of immune-cell dynamics to explain how organ-specific inflammation controls infection, causes collateral injury and transitions toward repair.

current_direction.headline: Immune adaptation, immunothrombosis and repair
current_direction.summary: Recent work points toward understanding how resident macrophages, neutrophils, platelets and recruited monocytes reorganize across infection or tissue damage—and how those dynamics might be redirected therapeutically.
current_direction.basis: Synthesized from the cited recent publications; not presented as a researcher-declared plan.
